children: SEBI accpets settlement. Nippon India MF to pay about Rs 92.46 crore. CEO Sundeep Sikka and fund manager Amit Tripathi to pay Rs 2.1 crore each. Total nears Rs 97 crore, sources say.
Despite there being a CBI probe, SEBI has settled.
The order is expected any time soon.
India's market regulator SEBI has approved a consent settlement with Nippon India Mutual Fund and three of its top executives.

The case concerns the fund house's investments in Additional Tier-1 (AT1) bonds of Yes Bank. It closes a show cause notice that the regulator issued about two years ago, according to people familiar with the matter. While the The show cause notice was issued two years ago, yet in all that time neither the fund house nor its executives filed a reply, and SEBI did not press them to, sources said.
Two years, no replies. Would a smaller player have been given the same room? It's a question the rest of the industry may well be asking.

Under the settlement, Nippon Life India Asset Management will pay about Rs 92.46 crore, sources said. Sundeep Sikka, the fund house's CEO and currently chairman of the Association of Mutual Funds in India (AMFI), will pay Rs 2.1 crore. Head fund manager Amit Tripathi will also pay Rs 2.1 crore, and former chief risk officer Milind Nesarikar will pay Rs 25.83 lakh. Altogether, the total is roughly Rs 97 crore.
Sources put the overall figure in the Rs 97–100 crore range.

As with all consent settlements under SEBI's Settlement Proceedings Regulations, the applicants pay the settlement amount without admitting or denying the charges. Once the order is passed, SEBI's proceedings against them end. This is the market regulator's version of "let's agree to stop talking about it."
The file that changed desks
Settlement orders are signed by SEBI's whole-time members.
This one reportedly took a slightly scenic route to get there.

The file first went to whole-time member Varshney, sources say. He recused himself because only a few days remained in his term at the time, and he later received an extension. The file then moved to KVR Murthy, who signed it along with fellow whole-time member Sandip Pradhan, sources said.
Nothing in SEBI's rules stops a file from finding a new signatory.
But in a matter this sensitive, it is the kind of detail market watchers will note.
Meanwhile, at the CBI
The settlement sits awkwardly alongside a criminal case that shows no sign of settling.

The CBI has already filed a chargesheet in the case. It relates to an alleged Rs 2,797-crore quid pro quo arrangement linking Reliance Nippon Mutual Fund, as the fund house was then known, with Yes Bank. The agency has charged former Yes Bank chief Rana Kapoor and industrialist Anil Ambani.
Sources said the agency is also examining the alleged misuse of EPFO funds and is expected to file another chargesheet.

A SEBI settlement closes SEBI's own proceedings. It does not bind the CBI, and it does not affect a criminal prosecution. So the regulator has closed its case while the investigating agency keeps adding to its own.
Several legal experts said this sequence could set an uncomfortable precedent. If a regulator settles while a criminal probe on the same facts is still under way, it risks sending mixed signals.
Optics may matter after all.
Two Applicants In, Two Out
In the same matter, SEBI rejected the settlement applications of Anil Ambani and Rana Kapoor, sources said.

Securities lawyers said the split outcome is likely to be challenged. Both men could argue before the Securities Appellate Tribunal or the courts that applicants in the same transaction were treated differently.
A regulator with SEBI's experience would be well aware of that possibility, one lawyer said. The more interesting question is how it plans to defend the distinction.

The applications were reviewed by SEBI's High Powered Advisory Committee (HPAC) on settlement orders and compounding of offences. The committee is headed by Justice Jai Narayan Patel, former Chief Justice of the Calcutta High Court.

Its other members are P.K. Malhotra, former Law Secretary; S.K. Mohanty, IRS (retd.) and a former SEBI whole-time member; and N. Venkatram, former managing partner and CEO of Deloitte India. The committee recommends settlement terms, and whole-time members make the final decision.
Sayonara, Show Cause Notice
The timing, sources point out, could hardly be more cordial.
India–Japan ties have been warming steadily.

On July 22, Japan's Consul-General in Mumbai, Sato Hitomi, paid a courtesy call on SEBI chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey. According to the Japanese consulate, the two sides discussed financial sector activity and cooperation between the two countries.
Nippon Life, the Japanese parent of the fund house, is also hosting a cricket match between India and Japan, sources said.

SEBI's chairman recently visited a Nippon India branch in a north Indian state.  SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey visited Leh, Jammu and Kashmir/Ladakh region in September 2026 to address an Investor Awareness Programme organized by AMFI for Army personnel.
A settlement with one of Japan's largest financial groups "could go a long way" for the bilateral relationship, one person familiar with the matter said.
Nobody is suggesting any connection between these developments, of course. They are simply coincidences.
For Sikka, the settlement removes a regulatory cloud at a time when his profile has never been higher. As AMFI chairman, he is the public face of an industry that manages over Rs 75 lakh crore.
Next in Line: Quant
The Nippon order may not be the only big settlement this season.
SEBI is also expected to decide on a settlement application from Quant Mutual Fund in a front-running case, sources said.

This epiphany fueled his pivot to financial journalism, where he’s spent years decoding the complex machinations of India’s ‘white money’ economy.

From stock market manipulations to regulatory loopholes, Palak’s work peels back the polished veneer of high finance to reveal the cabals pulling the strings. His passion for uncovering truth, backed by a knack for connecting dots others miss, makes him a formidable voice in Indian journalism, unafraid to challenge the status quo and expose the players who think they’re untouchable.
